To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

aPKC isoform activation is required for insulin-stimulation of glucose transport in muscle and adipocytes and that aPKC activation and function are compromised in various states and models of insulin resistance.

aPKCs play an obligatory role for insulin- and exercise-stimulated glucose uptake in skeletal muscle and that aPKC activation in this tissue is compromised in various models of insulin resistance, including type 2 diabetes.
aPKCs serve as molecular switches to activate glucose transport in insulin-responsive tissues and that insulin-stimultated aPKC activation may be compromised in various states or insulin resistance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms of insulin and exercise-induced glucose transport in skeletal and cardiac muscle, and with the role of aPKCs in these responses.
the function and dysfunction of a specific family of protein kinases, the aPKCs, for glucose transport responses in insulin-sensitive and -resistant states.
the function and dysfunction of a novel family of kinases, aPKCs, for glucose transport in normal and pathophysiological states.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

aPKCs play a central role in the regulation of glucose transport and, as such, are critical for the maintenance of normal glucose homeostasis and for the prevention and/or the treatment of insulin resistance and diabetes.
aPKCs serve as molecular switches for insulin-stimulating glucose transport responses, while aPKC dysfunction may be a key mechanism for insulin resistance.

the role of aPKCs for insulin-stimulat-ed glucose transport in skeletal and cardiac muscle and adipocytes is not only to serve as a molecular link downstream of PI 3-ki-nase, but also to serve as a terminal switch for the initiation of insulin-stimulated translocation of GLUT4-containing vesicles to the plasma membrane.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the insulin-stimulated activation of aPKCs is required for insulin-stimulation of glucose transport in insulin-resistant states.

aPKCs serve downstream of multiple insulin-signaling pathways to activate glucose transport in insulin-stimulated and non-insulin-stimulated states and that aPKC activation may be compromised in insulin-resistant states.
aPKCs serve as molecular switches for glucose transport, and that aPKC dysfunction contributes to insulin resistance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the aPKC family of serine/threonine kinases is a critical component of insulin action in insulin-sensitive and -resistant states.
aPKCs, serving downstream of multiple signaling pathways, are required and sufficient for insulin-stimulted glucose transport.
aPKCs serve as critical molecular links between upstream signaling pathways and downstream metabolic responses in insulin-sensitive and -resistant cells.
